title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
Context (pp. 159–161): Euler has just argued, wrongly, that natural curvature of a rod does not change its tones. He therefore treats a closed elastic ring (a circle or any closed curve of perimeter a) as a straight beam whose arc length s runs round the loop. In modern terms he uses the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation, with the transverse displacement measured along the curve and curvature coupling ignored. For a normal mode with time factor sin(ζ + t√(2g/k)), the spatial factor is y(s) = α e^{s/f} + β e^{-s/f} + γ sin(s/f) + δ cos(s/f), where f^4 = b c² k (§53).

On this page (§54) he looks for boundary conditions. A closed ring has no free, simply supported or clamped ends. He uses the closure instead. Choose the origin A (s = 0) so that y(0) = 0; then α + β + δ = 0. Since s = a, 2a, 3a, … return to A, he requires y(na) = 0 for every n, with ω = a/f. The exponential terms grow or decay geometrically in n, so they cannot cancel the bounded trigonometric terms for all n; hence α = β = 0, then δ = 0, and γ sin(nω) = 0 for all n. So sin ω = 0, i.e. ω = iπ for integer i.

Then f = a/(iπ). The 'sonus' (Euler counts half-periods per unit time, i.e. √(2g/k)/π) equals c√(2gb)/(π f²) = i² π c√(2gb)/a². The ring's simple tones therefore go as 1 : 4 : 9 : 16 …

In §55 he draws conclusions:
- Only the fundamental and the double octave are audible, so rings, discs and bell-shaped dishes give especially pure, agreeable tones.
- Pitch varies as the inverse square of the perimeter.

The page serves the 'coronis' of E526: the sounds of elastic rings and, by suggestion, bells.
errors: Inadequate closure conditions. Euler imposes only y(na) = 0, i.e. periodicity of y at a single point. He omits continuity (periodicity) of slope, bending moment and shear force at the joint. For odd i, sin(iπ s/a) is antiperiodic: y(s+a) = −y(s), so the slope at A jumps from iπ/a to −iπ/a. The correct periodic conditions y^{(k)}(s+a) = y^{(k)}(s), k = 0..3, give a/f = 2nπ, with both sin and cos admissible (degenerate pairs). Even within his own straight-beam model, the odd i 'modes' are spurious. The lowest admissible tone is 4π c√(2gb)/a², four times the value he calls the fundamental.

The prior assumption (end of §52, p.159) that natural curvature does not affect the tones is false for a ring. It couples bending to extension and makes n = 1 a rigid-body motion. The correct thin-ring in-plane flexural frequencies (Hoppe 1871) are proportional to n(n²−1)/√(n²+1), n = 2, 3, …. Their ratios are about 1 : 2.83 : 5.42, not 1 : 4 : 9. Euler's acoustic conclusion that rings and bells sound 'purer' through a double-octave overtone is therefore unfounded.

The step 'α = β = δ = 0' is valid given his conditions. But choosing y(0) = 0 is only a phase normalization, which is legitimate only if the mode family is correctly identified. Because of the antiperiodicity issue above it was not.

ideas.what: Treating a closed ring as a beam with periodic (closure) boundary conditions in arc length
ideas.modern_name: Periodic boundary conditions for the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation on a circle
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (ring/bell theory, E303, 1766); correct curved-ring theory to Hoppe (1871), later Rayleigh and Love
ideas.where_published: E303 'Tentamen de sono campanarum' (Novi Comm. Petrop. 10, 1766) treats bells as stacks of rings; E526 (Acta Petrop. 1779/1782) this section

ideas.what: Excluding exponential (hyperbolic) solutions on a closed loop because they grow geometrically with the number of circuits
ideas.modern_name: Only bounded/periodic eigenfunctions survive on a compact periodic domain (Floquet multiplier 1)

ideas.what: Ring frequencies scale as i²/a² (inverse square of perimeter), overtones in square-number ratios
ideas.modern_name: Flexural frequency scaling of thin beams/rings (correct overtone law differs: Hoppe)
ideas.where_published: E526 §§54–55; scaling for straight rods earlier in E526 and in Euler's 1730s–1740s rod-vibration work

ideas.what: Suggestion that discs and bell-shaped dishes behave like rings and give 'purer' tones
ideas.usually_credited_to: Chladni (1787) experiments; Jakob II Bernoulli (1789) plates; Germain/Kirchhoff plate theory

deep.surprise_reason: The ring-as-periodic-beam idea is already in Euler's bell paper E303. Its defects (wrong closure conditions, neglect of curvature, wrong overtone series) are the known shortcomings that Hoppe and later Rayleigh corrected. The spurious odd modes from imposing only y(na) = 0 are a small, checkable flaw rather than an overlooked result. Nothing here appears absent from the historical record in a way that would surprise a specialist.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image. Minor point: in the final progression the fourth denominator is printed with a stray bracket ('|aa'), which is a print artifact for aa. The 'nus' in 'so-nus' continues across the line break as transcribed.
